question: What was making the strange radio bursts at the Parkes telescope that looked like signals from deep space, and how did finding out help real astronomy?

facts.fact: Lorimer and colleagues reported in 2007 a bright, millisecond radio burst found in archival Parkes survey data that they argued came from outside our galaxy.
facts.quote: we have discovered a 30-Jy dispersed burst of duration <5 ms located three degrees from the Small Magellanic Cloud

facts.fact: That first fast radio burst actually happened in 2001 and was spotted six years later in old Parkes data.
facts.quote: The first FRB was found in 2007. It actually occurred in 2001, but was discovered six years later during a more close and careful inspection of archival data from the Parkes radio telescope.

facts.fact: As part of her PhD at Swinburne, Sarah Burke-Spolaor searched old data sets for more bursts and instead found strange new signals she called perytons.
facts.quote: Instead of finding undiscovered FRBs, she found these strange new signals that she called perytons. They were like FRBs, but different.

facts.fact: Burke-Spolaor's team reported 16 pulses whose frequency sweep resembled the Lorimer Burst but which were clearly of terrestrial origin.
facts.quote: We report here on the detection of 16 pulses, the bulk of which exhibit a frequency sweep with a shape and magnitude resembling the Lorimer Burst.

facts.fact: Those look-alike signals cast doubt on whether the original burst really came from outside the galaxy.
facts.quote: The new detections cast doubt on the extragalactic interpretation of the original burst

facts.fact: Perytons showed up in all 13 beams of the Parkes receiver at once, which showed they came from Earth.
facts.quote: they didn’t pass the second; they were in all 13 beams at once. So the signals had to be coming from Earth, that much was clear.

facts.fact: The name peryton comes from a mythical winged elk that casts the shadow of a man, chosen because nobody knew what made the signals.
facts.quote: the name peryton was chosen from mythology to be unassociated with an exact physical phenomenon, due to the ambiguous origin of the detections. Perytons are winged elk that cast the shadow of a man.

facts.fact: Until the perytons were explained, astronomers couldn't be confident that fast radio bursts were real signals from space.
facts.quote: “Until the peryton mystery was solved, there was no way we could feel confident that what we were looking for were FRBs,” says Petroff.

facts.fact: The perytons in the literature happened only during office hours and mostly on weekdays.
facts.quote: the 25 perytons reported in the literature occured only during office hours and predominantly on weekdays.

facts.fact: Of the 46 perytons detected at Parkes since 1998, 16 came within just seven minutes on 23 June 1998.
facts.quote: Of the 46 perytons detected at Parkes since 1998 some 16, more than a third of the total, occurred within a period of just seven minutes, on 23rd June 1998.

facts.fact: Emily Petroff, a PhD student at Swinburne, led the hunt for the source of the perytons as part of her PhD.
facts.quote: Petroff led the charge on the hunt for the perytons’ source as part of her PhD work

facts.fact: Three new perytons turned up at Parkes in the week of 19 January 2015, each found within a day of happening.
facts.quote: Three new perytons were spotted in our data at Parkes during the week of January 19. Each one was discovered within a day of when it happened thanks to advances in data processing used at Parkes.

facts.fact: Swinburne's Andrew Jameson had recently built a real-time system meant to catch fast radio bursts, and it picked up the perytons too.
facts.quote: Swinburne’s Jameson had recently created a real-time detection system that was designed to detect FRBs, but proved useful for picking up perytons.

facts.fact: Petroff phoned the observatory to ask whether anything unusual, like construction or a film crew, had happened that week; nothing had.
facts.quote: Petroff called the observatory scientists in the hope of finding a possible cause for these — construction, a film crew or anything else out of the ordinary. None of these had occurred.

facts.fact: CSIRO had installed a radio interference monitor at Parkes in December 2014.
facts.quote: In December 2014 CSIRO installed a radio frequency interference (RFI) monitor at the Parkes site to monitor the RFI environment around the telescope.

facts.fact: The monitor showed a burst of radio emission around 2.5 GHz at the time of each peryton, outside the band the telescope was observing.
facts.quote: at the time of each peryton event, there was also a period of radio emission at the frequency 2.5 GHz, out of the range we were observing with the telescope.

facts.fact: The paper puts that emission in the range 2.3 to 2.5 GHz, matching the timing of the perytons to within one time sample.
facts.quote: events the Parkes RFI monitor detected emission in the frequency range 2.3 ∼ 2.5 GHz consistent (to less than one time sample) with the time of the 1.4 GHz peryton event.

facts.fact: The most notorious household device emitting at that frequency is the microwave oven, so the team began testing the ovens on site.
facts.quote: Many consumer electronics emit at 2.5 GHz and the most notorious of these is the microwave oven. So we began to test the microwave ovens on site

facts.fact: There is no WiFi at Parkes, and there were few mobile phones around in 1998.
facts.quote: There is no WiFi at Parkes, and there were few cell phones around in 1998, when the first peryton was detected.

facts.fact: The 2.3 to 2.5 GHz spikes clustered in the daytime, between 9am and 5pm local time.
facts.quote: These events cluster in time of day and are much more common during daytime (between the hours of 9am and 5pm local time).

facts.fact: In the tests the load in the microwave was a ceramic mug full of water.
facts.quote: In each test the load in the microwave was a ceramic mug full of water.

facts.fact: Running the microwaves normally produced no perytons from either oven.
facts.quote: Our initial tests of running the microwave oven in a normal mode were unsuccessful and we didn’t see any perytons from either of the microwave ovens.

facts.fact: For weeks, dozens of microwave cycles failed to show up on the telescope's receiver.
facts.quote: Dozens of microwave cycles remained unregistered on the telescope’s receiver for weeks.

facts.fact: Parkes operations scientist John Sarkissian and director of operations John Reynolds ran the experiment heating mugs of water in the kitchen microwave.
facts.quote: the observatory’s operations scientist John Sarkissian and director of operations John Reynolds had been running an unusual experiment — heating up mugs of water in the facility’s kitchen microwave.

facts.fact: On 17 March 2015, John Reynolds suggested opening the microwave door before the cycle had finished, and a peryton appeared.
facts.quote: That was until 17 March 2015, when Reynolds made an off-the-wall suggestion to open the microwave door before the cycle had finished. Bingo.

facts.fact: That test produced 3 bright perytons from the staff kitchen microwave, each at the exact moment the door was opened.
facts.quote: This test produced 3 bright perytons from the staff kitchen microwave all at the exact times of opening the microwave oven door

facts.fact: The staff kitchen is in a building traditionally called the Woolshed.
facts.quote: the staff kitchen located in the building traditionally referred to as the Woolshed.

facts.fact: The Woolshed is about 100 m from the dish.
facts.quote: for the Woolshed (located 100m from the Dish at an azimuth of 65◦ )

facts.fact: A peryton is only seen when the microwave has a direct line of sight to the receiver, not blocked by the dish surface, and the oven is stopped by opening the door.
facts.quote: We found that we could generate perytons in our data by simply having a direct line of sight between the microwave oven and the telescope receiver (without the telescope surface itself in the way) and stopping the microwave oven by opening the door.

facts.fact: Opening the door early made a peryton only about half the time.
facts.quote: perytons appear to be generated with a ∼50% success rate.

facts.fact: Radio emission escaping from the oven while its magnetron shuts down explains all the observed properties of perytons.
facts.quote: Radio emission escaping from microwave ovens during the magnetron shut-down phase neatly explain all of the observed properties of the peryton signals.

facts.fact: Petroff was at an airport layover in Singapore in March 2015 when an email from her collaborators told her the answer.
facts.quote: But during a stop in Singapore in March 2015, astrophysicist Emily Petroff gasped as she opened her laptop. An email from her collaborators in Melbourne revealed the answer to a significant mystery she’d been trying to solve.

facts.fact: Swinburne astrophysicists Andrew Jameson, Ewan Barr and Evan Keane analysed the test data and confirmed the microwave was the source.
facts.quote: astrophysicists Andrew Jameson, Ewan Barr and Evan Keane, then analysed the signals detected by the telescope during these tests, they confirmed that the microwave was indeed the source.

facts.fact: Petroff wrote most of the paper reporting the discovery on her flight back to Melbourne.
facts.quote: Petroff wrote most of the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society paper reporting the discovery on her flight back to Melbourne.

facts.fact: The two ovens responsible were both made by Matsushita/National and were more than 27 years old but still working.
facts.quote: The two ovens responsible for most or all of the observed perytons are from the same manufacturer (Matsushita/National) and are both in excess of 27 years of age though still working reliably.

facts.fact: The paper by Petroff and 14 co-authors was published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
facts.quote: In a paper to be published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and available on Arxiv here, Petroff and 14 others nailed down the characteristics of perytons that suggest they come from microwave ovens.

facts.fact: The team showed the on-site microwaves could not have caused the first fast radio burst, FRB 010724.
facts.quote: we furthermore demonstrate that the microwaves on site could not have caused FRB 010724.

facts.fact: The first fast radio burst, FRB 010724, happened at 5:50 am local time, when the visitors centre was closed and unstaffed.
facts.quote: Additionally, the event occurred at 19:50 UT, i.e., 5:50 am AEST, when the visitors centre is closed and unstaffed.

facts.fact: The paper concluded that fast radio bursts are excellent candidates for genuine signals from beyond our galaxy.
facts.quote: This and other distinct observational differences show that FRBs are excellent candidates for genuine extragalactic transients.

facts.fact: Checking for simultaneous 2.3 to 2.5 GHz emission became a direct test to tell a peryton from a fast radio burst.
facts.quote: A direct test of “peryton vs. FRB” can be made via the detection or non-detection, respectively, of concurrent 2.3–2.5 GHz emission.

facts.fact: Petroff got the job in the Netherlands and went on to track real fast radio bursts.
facts.quote: Solving the mystery turned out to be a good omen for Petroff, who got the job in the Netherlands and now tracks real FRBs to their intergalactic sources.

facts.fact: In January 2017 researchers pinned one repeating fast radio burst, FRB 121102, to a dwarf galaxy billions of light-years away.
facts.quote: But researchers have now pinpointed the source of one series of the FRBs — to a dwarf galaxy billions of light-years away from Earth.

facts.fact: Petroff says the team always knew perytons came from nearby; the fun was in solving the puzzle.
facts.quote: We always knew perytons were coming from nearby; the real fun lay in putting all the pieces together to solve the puzzle.

people.name: Emily Petroff
people.role: Swinburne University PhD student (joint with CSIRO) who led the peryton hunt and was lead author of the 2015 paper
people.stake: Until perytons were explained, nobody could be confident the fast radio bursts she studied were real signals from space; her PhD work rode on it

people.name: John Reynolds
people.role: Director of operations at CSIRO's Parkes Observatory
people.stake: His site's telescope data was being muddied by an unexplained local signal; he suggested opening the microwave door early, the test that worked

people.name: John Sarkissian
people.stake: Ran the kitchen microwave experiments with Reynolds

people.name: Sarah Burke-Spolaor
people.role: Swinburne PhD student who found and named the perytons
people.stake: Her look-alike signals cast doubt on the first fast radio burst

people.name: D. R. Lorimer
people.role: Lead author of the 2007 paper reporting the first fast radio burst (the 'Lorimer Burst')
people.stake: Whether his burst was a real signal from beyond the galaxy

people.name: Andrew Jameson
people.role: Swinburne astrophysicist who built the real-time detection system and helped analyse the test data
people.stake: His new software caught the January 2015 perytons fast enough to investigate

timeline.what: 16 perytons hit the Parkes telescope within seven minutes
timeline.why: Unknown at the time; later traced to the Woolshed microwave

timeline.what: The first fast radio burst happens; Lorimer's team finds it in old Parkes data and reports it in 2007 as coming from outside the galaxy
timeline.why: Careful re-inspection of archival survey data

timeline.what: Sarah Burke-Spolaor searches old data for more bursts and finds 16 look-alike signals in all 13 beams; she names them perytons
timeline.why: She was hoping to find more fast radio bursts; the name was chosen because nobody knew what made them

timeline.what: Perytons cast doubt on whether fast radio bursts were real
timeline.why: They had the same frequency sweep as a signal from space

timeline.what: CSIRO installs a radio interference monitor at Parkes
timeline.why: To keep track of radio noise around the telescope

timeline.what: Three new perytons are caught within a day; Petroff asks the observatory if anything odd happened and learns of the new monitor
timeline.why: Jameson's real-time software found them fast enough to check what was happening on site

timeline.what: The monitor shows a 2.3 to 2.5 GHz burst at the moment of each peryton, so the team suspects the microwave ovens
timeline.why: The microwave oven is the most notorious device at that frequency; there is no WiFi at Parkes

timeline.what: Tests heating mugs of water in the site microwaves produce no perytons for weeks
timeline.why: The ovens were being run normally, to the end of their cycle

timeline.what: Reynolds suggests opening the door before the timer ends; the kitchen microwave produces 3 bright perytons, exactly when the door opens
timeline.why: Stopping the oven early lets radio emission from the shutting-down magnetron escape

timeline.what: Petroff learns the result by email during a Singapore layover and writes most of the paper on the flight home
timeline.why: She was returning from a job interview in the Netherlands

timeline.what: The paper shows the microwaves could not have made the first fast radio burst, so bursts are excellent candidates for real signals from space
timeline.why: FRB 010724 happened at 5:50 am, when the visitors centre was closed, and the paper found other clear differences between bursts and perytons

timeline.what: Researchers trace a repeating fast radio burst to a dwarf galaxy billions of light-years away

turn.what: On 17 March 2015, instead of letting the microwave finish, they opened the door early, and the telescope lit up with perytons at the exact moment the door opened. The 'signals from space' look-alikes were the staff kitchen microwave, which cleared the first fast radio burst and let astronomers trust that the real bursts come from beyond our galaxy.

key_objects: The Parkes radio telescope dish ('The Dish') in New South Wales, Australia
The 13-beam receiver in the focus cabin above the dish
A frequency-swept radio blip on a time-frequency plot (the peryton)
The radio interference monitor antenna installed in December 2014
An old Matsushita/National microwave oven in the staff kitchen
A ceramic mug full of water inside the microwave
The microwave door being opened before the timer hits zero
The Woolshed building, about 100 m from the dish
A laptop opened at an airport in Singapore
A distant dwarf galaxy (source of a real fast radio burst)
unverified: Wikipedia says 'the first signal occurred in 2001 but was not discovered until 2007' about perytons; that describes the first fast radio burst (Lorimer Burst), not a peryton. Perytons date back to at least 1998.

Retellings say the culprit was staff heating their lunch. The tests used mugs of water; lunch is inferred from the time-of-day clustering (and Nature Index's phrasing), not observed for any specific peryton. Say 'around lunchtime' at most.
'Scientists baffled by alien signals' framing: Petroff explicitly rejects it; the team always knew perytons were local. Do not imply anyone thought they were aliens.

Wikipedia and the Conversation give the frequency as 2.5 GHz; the paper gives 2.3-2.5 GHz. A '2,466 MHz' figure appears only as the centre of a plotting window in a figure caption, not as the ovens' frequency.
Who physically opened the microwave door on 17 March 2015 is not named; Nature Index credits Reynolds with the suggestion and says Sarkissian and Reynolds ran the experiment.

Number of microwaves: the Conversation says two on site (kitchen and visitors' centre); the paper says three near the telescope (tower, visitors centre, staff kitchen/Woolshed) plus two at the observers' quarters about 1 km away.
Nature Index says Burke-Spolaor found the signals 'in 2011'; her paper was submitted September 2010 and published 2011.
The 23 June 1998 cluster could not be reproduced by opening the door; the paper conjectures (untested) the operator compromised the shielding, perhaps with aluminium foil.
Claims that every peryton everywhere comes from microwave ovens: not checked (a 2019 arXiv paper on a peryton in China was seen in a search result but not opened).
'The mystery lasted 17 years' as a headline: the paper says perytons from at least two ovens were seen over 17 years (1998-2015), but this 'mystery' framing was not opened in a headline source.
The cause of fast radio bursts themselves remains unsolved per these sources; do not say the microwave work explained what FRBs are.
Lorimer's first name is not given on the pages opened (arXiv lists 'D. R. Lorimer').
